subtitle: Three shapes describe most of what we count and measure, and one theorem explains why the bell curve turns up everywhere.

disc.body:
Counting the number of buses that pass you in an hour is very different from measuring the exact time one arrives. The first gives whole numbers; the second can be anything on a scale. A discrete variable takes countable values and has a probability mass function p(x) with Σp = 1. A continuous variable has a density f(x) with total area 1; probabilities are areas, so P(X = a) = 0 and P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫f dx.

Both share a tool, the cdf F(x) = P(X ≤ x). Here is the surprise to remember: for a continuous X, the chance of exactly 2.5 is 0, because a single point has no area.
keynotes: A discrete variable takes countable values and has a probability mass function p(x) with Σp = 1.
A continuous variable has a density f(x) with total area 1; probabilities are areas, so P(X = a) = 0 and P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫f dx.
The cdf F(x) = P(X ≤ x) works for both.

binom.body:
Toss a coin 10 times: how many heads? That is the binomial question. With n independent trials, each succeeding with probability p, P(X = k) = ⁿCₖ pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, with mean np and variance np(1 − p). The chance of 4 to 6 heads in 10 fair tosses is 0.65625.

Do it by hand. P(X = 5) = ¹⁰C₅ (½)¹⁰ = 252/1024 ≈ 0.246. Add k = 4 and 6 (210/1024 each) and P(4 ≤ X ≤ 6) = 0.656. Shaded bars sum to the probability in the figure. And a binomial with n = 40, p = 0.25 has mean np = 10.
keynotes: Binomial: n independent trials with success probability p give P(X = k) = ⁿCₖ pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, mean np and variance np(1 − p).
For 10 fair coin tosses P(X = 5) = 252/1024 ≈ 0.246 and P(4 ≤ X ≤ 6) = 0.65625.
A binomial with n = 40 and p = 0.25 has mean 10.

pois.body:
What about events that arrive at random, like calls to a help-line or typos on a page? The Poisson distribution counts rare events in an interval. For events arriving independently at average rate λ per interval: P(X = k) = e⁻λ λᵏ/k!, with mean = variance = λ. It is the limit of the binomial as n → ∞, p → 0 with np = λ.

With λ = 4 calls per hour, P(at most 2 calls) = 0.2381; the bars for k = 0, 1, 2 are shaded in the figure. A Poisson variable has variance equal to its mean, λ, so you can recognise one from just two numbers.
keynotes: For events arriving independently at average rate λ per interval, P(X = k) = e⁻λ λᵏ/k! with mean = variance = λ.
It is the limit of the binomial as n → ∞ and p → 0 with np = λ.
With λ = 4 calls per hour, P(at most 2 calls) = 0.2381.

norm.body:
Now the star of statistics, the bell curve. f(x) = exp(−(x − μ)²/2σ²)/(σ√2π). To use it, standardise with z = (x − μ)/σ and read the standard table. Remember the 68–95–99.7 rule: P(|Z| ≤ 1) = 0.68269, P(|Z| ≤ 1.96) = 0.95, the central 95 % in the figure.

Try it. Heights ~ N(170, 10²). P(X > 185): z = (185 − 170)/10 = 1.5, and the tail area beyond 1.5 is 0.0668. And x = 55 from N(40, 5²) has z = (55 − 40)/5 = 3: three standard deviations out, which is very rare.
keynotes: The normal density is f(x) = exp(−(x − μ)²/2σ²)/(σ√2π); standardise with z = (x − μ)/σ and read the standard table.
For heights ~ N(170, 10²), P(X > 185) has z = 1.5 and tail area 0.0668.

approx.body:
Computing binomial probabilities for big n is tedious, but there is a shortcut you will love. When np and n(1 − p) are both at least about 5, Binomial(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). Step through n = 5, 10, 30 in the figure and watch the bars fit the curve ever better.

A small trick makes it accurate: apply a ±½ continuity correction when converting a count to a continuous area. So to approximate P(X ≤ 12) for a binomial by a normal, you use 12.5 as the cut-off.
keynotes: When np and n(1 − p) are both at least about 5, Binomial(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)).
The bars fit the curve ever better as n goes through 5, 10 and 30.
Apply a ±½ continuity correction when converting a count to a continuous area.

clt.body:
Here is why the bell curve is everywhere, and it is a small miracle. Take samples of size n from any population with mean μ and sd σ. The sample means X̄ are approximately N(μ, σ²/n) for large n, with standard error σ/√n.

See it with your own eyes: start from a lopsided exponential population; single draws have sd 1.034, yet means of 30 have sd 0.184 (theory 0.183) and a bell shape. The histogram of 400 sample means is symmetric in the figure. And since the standard error is σ/√n, quadrupling the sample size halves it.
keynotes: Samples of size n from any population with mean μ and sd σ have means X̄ approximately N(μ, σ²/n), with standard error σ/√n.
From a lopsided exponential population, single draws have sd 1.034 yet means of 30 have sd 0.184 (theory 0.183) and a bell shape.
Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error.
